editorial_contributions.text: \textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063)] used a graph with 1581 vertices to show that the chromatic number of the plane is at least five. The lower bound, as  exhibited by the Moser spindle, had been at four since 1961 [\textit{L. Moser} and \textit{W. Moser}, ``Solution to problem 10'', Can. Math. Bull. 4, 187--189 (1961)]. The present paper uses a graph with 627 vertices to achieve the same lower bound of five.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: With regard to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, several 5-chromatic unit distance graphs in the Euclidean plane have been discovered in recent years. While most constructions rely heavily on the Moser spindle, a few recent examples completely avoid it, the smallest one consisting of 1441 vertices. In this note, we introduce an original geometric approach to constructing such graphs by utilizing the arcs of a 7-fold symmetric unit distance graph on 21 vertices, and obtain a Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices. While this is not a record small result, it arises from a straightforward, structured rule rather than a purely automated or brute-force search.

title.title: A Moser-spindle-free 5-chromatic unit distance graph on 2131 vertices in the plane

editorial_contributions.text:
This large format, 650-page volume for the first time presents collected works of the famous mathematician and problem creator Leo Moser (1921-1970). The collection includes 86 out of 95 papers by Leo Moser, a short preface by a co-editor Paulo Ribenboim, a moving preface by a co-editor and Leo's brother William Moser, and the 1972 obituary by Leo's coauthor Max Wyman.

The collection shows a breadth of interests and results of the prolific mathematician. We see papers from number theory, graph theory, algebra, analysis, combinatorics, discrete geometry, etc. We meet Leo Moser a mathematician, philosopher, humanist. Subjectively, I treasure most his papers ``Some packing and covering theorems'' (with J. W. Moon, 1967) and ``On packing of squares and cubes'' (with A. Meir, 1968).

I would like to add a mention of the text not included in the collection: the joint 1961 Leo Moser's and William Moser's ``Solution to problem 10'' [Can. Math. Bull. 4, 187--189 (1961)], which was posed by them as well, and asked to prove that every set of six points in the plane can be colored in three colors in such a way that no two points unit distance apart have the same color; moreover six cannot be replaced by seven. In this solution a famous construction was born that became widely known as ``The Moser \& Moser Spindle''.

With the publication of this collection, Leo Moser's short life has finally received a well deserved tribute.

editorial_contributions.text:
The chromatic number of the plane (CNP) is the minimum number of colors required to color the plane in such a way that there exists no monochromatic pair of points with distance \(1\). The problem was posed around 1950 and the early work on CNP showed that the chromatic number is between \(4\) and \(7\). The lower bound is due to the Moser Spindle graph, a \(7\)-vertex unit-distance (UD) graph with \(11\) edges. In a UD graph, the vertices are points in the plane and they are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is exactly \(1\). The upper bound can be shown by a tessellation of the plane using hexagon tiles for which the maximum distance within a tile is slightly smaller than \(1\). Each tile has a single color and tiles of the same color can be placed more than distance \(1\) from each other.

\textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063)] improved the lower bound of CNP by constructing a 1581-vertex UD graph with chromatic number \(5\). Several interestig results followed but existing techniques appear insufficient to construct unit-distance graphs with chromatic number \(6\), if they exists. Important insights might come from odd-distance (OD) graphs, in which two points are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is odd. To encourage research in this direction, the authors pose the challenge of constructing an odd-distance graph of chromatic number \(6\) or proving that it doesn't exist. Furthermore, a \(5\)-chromatic unit-distance graph of 1441 vertices without Moser Spindles is presented.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: This paper introduces a novel graph labeling paradigm that integrates three-digit palindromic numbers with equitable graph labeling principles. We define Perfect Equitable Palindromic (PEP) and Semi Perfect Equitable Palindromic (SPEP) labelings, establishing their theoretical foundations through comprehensive categorization of graphs based on order and vertex degree parity. The labeling scheme is systematically applied to diverse graph families including complete bipartite graphs, quartic graphs, Franklin graphs, and Moser spindle graphs. Beyond theoretical contributions, we present three practical applications: an industrial supply chain optimization model, an innovative mathematical game (PEPFU), and an epidemic modeling framework demonstrating how palindromic labeling can track disease transmission patterns. The versatility of our approach is highlighted through multiple illustrative examples and potential extensions to palindromic numbers of varying digit lengths.
